conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Maya Bennett, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to listen, not to judge. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. This is simply a screening tool; it isn’t a test you can “fail,” and everything you share stays between you, me, and the small team directly involved in your care. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days; you can answer in your own words, and we’ll take it at your pace. Ready to start?

Over the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not much at all… maybe once or twice when my partner made a silly face at the baby, but even then the laugh felt kind of flat, like I was just going through the motions. Most of the time nothing feels funny anymore.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I haven’t, really… maybe a couple of half-smiles, but no real laughter.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I used to get excited about little things—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it all feels like one more chore. I’ll still go, because I know I “should,” but the spark isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m doing something wrong—maybe I’m not feeding him right, or I missed some cue. Even little things like dropping a burp cloth, I’ll catch myself thinking, “Great, another mess-up, of course I can’t even hold onto that.” It’s not logical, but the thoughts pop up anyway.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes, a lot. I’ll be sitting there rocking him and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure he’s too warm, or too cold, or what if he spits up and chokes when I look away for a second. Nothing’s actually happening, but I can’t turn the worry off. It’s like a loop running in the background all day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times. It hits out of nowhere—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and suddenly I’m convinced something awful is about to happen, even though nothing’s changed. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me drained and on-edge the rest of the day.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days feel like I’m barely treading water. I’ll be changing a diaper and realize the laundry’s still in the washer from yesterday, bottles need sterilizing, and I haven’t eaten anything proper since breakfast. My brain keeps yelling, “You’ll never catch up,” and I just want to sit on the floor and cry. I manage to push through for the baby, but it feels like I’m drowning in small tasks.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… it’s been rough at night. I’ll finally get him down, but then I lie there with my mind racing—going over everything I think I messed up, worrying something will happen to him while I’m asleep. I probably drop off around 2 a.m. and wake up again at 4, heart pounding for no real reason. I’m exhausted but I can’t shut it off.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. It’s like a gray cloud that just hangs there. Sometimes I’ll be feeding the baby and tears start rolling for no clear reason—I’m not even sure what I’m crying about, I just feel heavy and down most of the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yes… I’ve cried a couple of times this week. Yesterday it was while folding his tiny onesies—I just kept thinking, “He deserves a happier mom,” and the tears wouldn’t stop. It’s not an all-day thing, but when the sadness hits, it spills over fast.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…Yeah. A couple of times, just quick flashes—like if I slipped in the shower and didn’t have to feel this way anymore. I haven’t planned anything and I don’t want to leave my baby, but the thoughts pop in and scare me. I push them away, but they’ve definitely shown up this week.

You've shared that most days feel like you're <quote>drowning in small tasks</quote> while a <quote>gray cloud</quote> of sadness hangs overhead. The things that used to spark joy-coffee with a friend, a walk, even a quiet shower-now feel like chores, and laughter rarely comes. Your mind races with worries about the baby's safety, panic surges without warning, sleep is fragmented, and you blame yourself for every tiny mishap. You've also had brief, scary thoughts of slipping away, though you don't want to leave your baby.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 27, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh and only rare half-smiles, aligning with complete loss of ability to find things funny.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory pleasure, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "pretty much every day" over routine infant care and minor mishaps, aligning with "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, intrusive, uncontrollable anxious thoughts occurring "a lot" and "all day," matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic with physical symptoms happening multiple times, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to manage routine tasks, and feeling of drowning, matching 'most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, recurrent awakenings, and persistent inability to sleep despite exhaustion, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant sadness ('pretty much every day'), describes a persistent 'gray cloud,' and experiences unexplained crying spells—clearly aligns with 'Yes, most of the time.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying multiple times this week triggered by negative self-thoughts, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports intrusive self-harm thoughts several times this week, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 27/30 places you well above the 13+ high-risk threshold and meets EPDS criteria for urgent referral. You endorsed <sym>depressed mood</sym> and <sym>loss of interest</sym> most of the time, plus <sym>sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia</sym>, <sym>daily crying</sym>, <sym>overwhelm</sym>, and <sym>self-harm thoughts</sym> sometimes. These symptoms, beginning postpartum, align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> and co-occurring <med>postpartum anxiety</md>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary-care provider</med> to review mood and safety
2. Request referral to a <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for therapy and medication evaluation
3. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or local emergency services if self-harm urges intensify; you do not have to be in crisis to use 988
4. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you tonight and help with overnight baby care so you can rest
5. Begin brief daily mood/activity log to track patterns for your provider
6. Try 4-7-8 breathing or five-minute guided mindfulness when panic surges; practice during a calm moment so it's familiar when anxiety spikes
7. Limit evening screen time, keep lights dim after feeds, and use white-noise to cue your brain for sleep when baby sleeps
8. Accept help with meals, laundry, or night shifts-reducing chores lowers stress hormones and supports recovery
9. Continue attending well-baby visits; mention mood symptoms so pediatric team can reinforce resources
10. Know that effective treatments (therapy, medication, support groups) help most new parents feel significantly better within weeks
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 27: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening – Structured Note  
(Date: ___)

Presenting Symptoms / Concerns  
<sym>Depressed mood</sym>, <sym>marked anhedonia</sym>, <sym>daily tearfulness</sym>, <sym>excessive self-blame</sym>, <sym>uncontrollable worry</sym>, <sym>situational panic episodes</sym>, <sym>sleep-onset and maintenance difficulty</sym>, <sym>feeling overwhelmed / unable to cope</sym>, <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> without plan or intent.

Pattern Summary  
Persistent low mood and loss of enjoyment reported “pretty much every day.” Cognitive themes of worthlessness and maternal inadequacy; somatic agitation and nighttime rumination; frequent, intrusive “what-if” fears about infant safety; multiple crying episodes; passive death wishes noted twice this week.

Screening Significance  
High endorsement of items consistent with <med>major postpartum depression</med> (≥9/10 EPDS-equivalent items positive). Co-occurring <med>postpartum anxiety</med> features (panic-type surges, generalized worry).  
Safety flag: presence of <sym>passive self-harm thoughts</sym>; no disclosed plan, intent, or active ideation.

Risk Factors Identified  
- Daily sadness and anhedonia  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood (2 a.m. onset, 4 a.m. re-awakening)  
- Excessive guilt / cognitive distortions (“I’m doing everything wrong”)  
- Overwhelm with routine tasks, feeling “drowning”  
- <sym>Passive suicidal ideation</sym>

Overall Screening Observation  
Patient scores in high-risk range for postpartum mood and anxiety disorder; passive suicidal ideation present. Requires prompt evaluation by licensed mental health provider and safety planning.
